transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-22
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood SE), Mark Chen (Aurora CTO), Sofia Alvarez (Aurora Eng Mgr), Ravi Kumar (Aurora Data Scientist), Emily Park (Aurora Product)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping and integration planning for Aurora's customer support summarization use case. Discussed success criteria (latency, accuracy, hallucination thresholds), workload sizing (concurrent users, seq lengths), benchmarking plan and timelines, and integration options (Redwood SDKs, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function/tool calling for structured output). Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Success criteria and eval metrics
- Workload sizing and throughput expectations
- Benchmark harness, datasets, and acceptance thresholds
- Integration: SDKs vs direct OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function/tool calling, structured JSON outputs
- Security: VPC/private deployment considerations, KMS, audit logs

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect in places)
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining \u2014 I'm Jordan Lee from Redwood, AE on this account, with Priya and Marta from our solutions team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Mark: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to get this scoped.
[00:11] Sofia: Yep, thanks for setting this up. We want to make sure the POC maps to our production traffic and that the integration is minimal for our eng team.
[00:20] Priya: Totally. High-level, I want to cover three things \u2014 success criteria (what you consider a win), workload sizing (what does production look like), and the benchmarks we should run, then talk integration paths and what sample artifacts you can share. Sound good?
[00:33] Emily: Perfect. We'll start with success criteria.
[00:36] Ravi: For us the key deliverable is a summarized ticket output that matches our current rubric: precision on named entities, no critical hallucination, and response latency under 500ms median for short tickets and under 1200ms for long threads. If we hit those two most of our PMs will be happy.
[00:51] Priya: Great, that is specific \u2014 you mentioned entity precision and hallucination thresholds, do you have numeric targets?
[00:55] Ravi: Target for named-entity precision 92%+, hallucination (defined as unsupported facts) under 3% on the eval set. Those are our bar.
[01:04] Jordan: Noted. From Redwood's side we'll run both hosted and a dedicated private benchmark so you see the economics and the latency tradeoff. For integration, do you want to call our OpenAI-compatible endpoints or embed our SDK?
[01:17] Mark: Ideally minimal changes, so if the OpenAI-compatible endpoints mirror the calls we already have, that's easiest for the team. But we do want function/tool calling for structured JSON output \u2014 that's critical to slot into our ingestion pipeline.
[01:29] Priya: We support OpenAI-compatible endpoints and our SDKs. The function-calling pattern works with both, and we can also return structured JSON via schema-guided generation. Sometimes transcription will show it as a function call or tool call, so there might be small name mismatches, e.g., our docs show 'tool' and some clients call it 'function'. We'll include example payloads.
[01:52] Sofia: On throughput \u2014 our peak is about 120 concurrent agents making requests, average ticket length 400 tokens, peak 1,200 tokens. We expect bursts up to 250 concurrent for release days.
[02:05] Priya: That helps a lot. For benchmarking we'll simulate that concurrency profile and run both batch and streaming modes. Which is more important for you: cost per token minimization or strict latency SLAs?
[02:17] Mark: Latency first, cost second; but show us both so stakeholders can decide.
[02:22] Jordan: Understood. We'll include cost/cpu numbers for hosted vs dedicated. Quick clarification \u2014 do you have any PII retention rules or data residency needs?
[02:31] Emily: Yes \u2014 tickets contain user PII and we need logs expired within 30 days and must be SOC2 equivalent; we also prefer EU routing for EU customers.
[02:40] Priya: We can do region pinning and S3 audit logs; Private deployment in your VPC is also an option for stricter control \u2014 that would be a separate pricing line. We'll share the SOC2 artifacts and our KMS integrations.
[02:52] Ravi: For evaluation, we have three prompt sets: short summary, summary-plus-actions, and thread-consolidation. We'll send examples. The short summary average is 350 tokens on input, expected output 120 tokens. Thread consolidation inputs up to 1,200 tokens.
[03:10] Jordan: Good. For benchmarks I'll outline two runs: 1) Latency focused run with synthetic concurrency and realistic token lengths, 2) Quality focused run against your labeled eval set to compute entity precision and hallucination rate. We'll include per-route token-level cost, and KV-cache/prefix caching impact.
[03:26] Sofia: For the quality run, can we run this on a dedicated node pool with the quantized model that mirrors what you'd run in production? We care about determinism.
[03:35] Priya: Yes \u2014 we can spin up a dedicated pool and pin the model/quantization profile. Note that quantization can affect hallucination slightly but improves throughput. We'll document the recommended profiles.
[03:45] Mark: About the integration \u2014 our stack is node + serverless workers. We prefer the npm SDK and will likely use your OpenAI-compatible endpoint as a fallback.
[03:56] Priya: Our Node SDK is published and we have example wrappers for serverless to avoid cold-start penalties; it includes streaming helpers and a function-calling wrapper to enforce JSON schema. For direct endpoint usage the call shape is compatible but you'll need to pass the schema in the prompt or use our function signature. We'll share code snippets.
[04:15] Emily: How do we handle tool calling that triggers downstream actions? For example, extract entities then call internal API to tag users. We want that to be auditable.
[04:23] Priya: Two options: 1) Return structured JSON and let your service call the internal APIs (simpler, auditable), or 2) use our tool-calling extension where Redwood can call back to a webhook you host. The callback approach is more integrated but requires setting up secure webhooks and auth. For POC we recommend returning structured JSON to keep it simple.
[04:44] Ravi: Agreed, structured JSON first. We'll evaluate webhook approach later.
[04:49] Jordan: On success criteria, we'll measure quality against your labeled set and produce a confusion-style report for named entity detection and hallucination cases, plus per-request latency distribution. Are there any other KPIs?
[04:59] Emily: Also measure end-to-end time including our ingestion and post-processing \u2014 in the lab you can simulate ours but we'll want a final run with our pipeline.
[05:08] Priya: We'll plan a final integrated run. For timelines, here's what I propose: you send prompt sets + sample data by 2027-07-24; we share benchmark harness by 2027-07-25; kickoff benchmark 2027-07-26; run through 2027-07-30 and share results early week of 2027-08-03. Does that timeline work?
[05:25] Mark: Sounds good to me. We may need a short technical session to set up VPC peering if we go that route.
[05:31] Jordan: We can schedule a VPC deep-dive if needed; it'll usually involve the security eng folks.
[05:36] Sofia: A couple of specific technical Qs: 1) How do you handle KV cache across sequences? 2) What's your approach to continuous batching vs guaranteed latency?
[05:45] Priya: KV cache is per-request session; if you use prefix caching for repeated context we can reuse the KV store which saves tokens. Continuous batching is workload-aware: we have a latency SLO that gates batching windows. For strict tail latency we reduce batch window and may fall back to smaller model variants.
[06:02] Ravi: Are there any gotchas with function-calling when using streaming? We saw some truncation issues elsewhere.
[06:07] Priya: Streaming plus function-calling is supported, but you need to finalize the schema validation on the client side. We stream token chunks and also a final 'function call completed' payload. The truncation you saw is usually due to client buffer handling \u2014 we'll share the client-side helpers.
[06:24] Jordan: We'll also include price estimates: hosted per-token and a dedicated reserved capacity breakdown. That way you can weigh cost vs latency.
[06:31] Mark: On encryption, we need BYOK / KMS integration for key management.
[06:35] Priya: We support KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments, and a managed KMS option for hosted with strict rotation; we'll include docs.
[06:45] Emily: What about audit logs and retention controls? We need to show auditors that logs are retained and purged according to policy.
[06:51] Marta: We surface audit logs per-request with IDs and can export them to your S3 with lifecycle policies. We'll include an example config.
[06:59] Sofia: For the benchmark harness, what OS/hardware will you run on? We want a comparable setup to our planned dedicated GPUs.
[07:05] Priya: We'll run hosted runs in our region-standard infra and the dedicated run on an n1-like GPU pool configured to match your planned instance types; we'll note the exact GPU, quantization and kernel selection in the report.
[07:18] Mark: Any limitation on token size for streaming or function calls?
[07:22] Priya: Technically we support up to 8k context in the plan we'll use; for longer threads we recommend chunking + summarization. If you need longer contexts, we can discuss using extended sequence profiles.
[07:33] Ravi: For the eval metrics, when you compute hallucination rate, please include examples in the report so we can triage and add examples to our prompt engineering set.
[07:41] Jordan: Absolutely \u2014 we provide a sample-of-errors section with categorized failure modes.
[07:47] Emily: Great. Anything else on integration?
[07:50] Priya: One more note \u2014 we have an OpenAPI-compatible shim for the function-call swagger so your platform can validate responses against a schema automatically. That usually reduces client-side parsing issues. We'll attach the examples.
[08:03] Mark: Ok let's recap next steps.
[08:06] Jordan: Recap: Aurora sends prompt sets and sample data by 2027-07-24; Priya will send benchmark harness + code samples and the Node SDK examples by 2027-07-25; Jordan will send POC scope & pricing by 2027-07-26; schedule benchmark run on 2027-07-26 and results by 2027-08-03. Action items in the notes.
[08:28] Mark: That aligns. We'll also confirm if we want private/VPC run for the dedicated benchmarks \u2014 we'll decide by 2027-07-24.
[08:39] Sofia: One small thing \u2014 our infra team needs the URLs and IP ranges for a short firewall whitelist.
[08:44] Marta: I'll send the IP ranges and a VPC peering doc in the email follow-up.
[08:49] Ravi: Quick question \u2014 do you have examples of structured output for named-entity extraction plus action items?
[08:55] Priya: Yes, we'll include JSON schema examples and a sample function signature.
[08:59] Emily: Thank you all, this was helpful.
[09:02] Jordan: Thanks everyone \u2014 we'll follow up with the docs and kickoff scheduling.
[09:07] Mark: Thanks, talk soon.

(End of transcript \u2014 transcription occasionally mis-heard technical terms like 'K-V cash' instead of KV cache; some speaker labels merged during recording.)
